blocks.text: A number of devices operate by means of the pressure difference that results from changes in the speed of the fluid.

The wing is designed to deflect the air so that the streamlines are closer together above the wing than below it. Where the streamlines are forced closer together the speed is faster, so air travels faster on the upper side of the wing than on the lower; the pressure is lower at the top of the wing, the wing is forced upward, and the lift of an aeroplane is due to this effect.

blocks.alt: A side view of the rear of an aeroplane with a wing section in front of it. Green streamlines from the left crowd closely together over the curved upper surface of the wing and stay spread out below it, all moving to the right. Red arrows under the wing point upward.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.17: Lift of an aeroplane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.17).

blocks.text: When a ball is thrown or kicked with spin, the ball is made smoother on one side by the bowler and remains rough on the other. The air moves faster over the rough side and slows over the smoother; by Bernoulli's equation the faster-moving air creates lower pressure while the slower air creates higher pressure, and this pressure difference generates a sideways force, the Magnus effect, which causes the ball to curve in the air.

blocks.alt: A ball in an air stream that moves from right to left. Above the ball the streamlines crowd together (Faster air, lower pressure); below it they spread out (Slower air, higher pressure). An arrow labelled Deflection force points up from the ball. An inset labelled Spinning ball shows a small spinning ball whose path curves up away from a dashed straight line.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.18: Turbulent flow (air flow past a spinning ball) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.18).

blocks.text: A filter pump has a constriction in the centre, so that a jet of water from the tap flows faster there. This causes a drop in pressure near it and air therefore flows in from the side tube; the air and water together are expelled through the lower part of the pump.

blocks.alt: A filter pump in section. Water enters a tube at the top labelled Water and is forced through a narrow nozzle into a fast jet that runs down the body of the pump and leaves at the bottom outlet. A side tube on the right, labelled Air flow, has an arrow showing air flowing in towards the jet.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.19: Turbulent flow (filter pump) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.19).

blocks.text: The carburetor of a car engine uses a Venturi duct to feed the correct mixture of air and petrol to the cylinders. Air is drawn through the duct and along a pipe to the cylinders, and a tiny inlet at the side of the duct is fed with petrol. The air through the duct moves very fast, creating low pressure in the duct, which draws petrol vapours into the air stream.

blocks.alt: A vertical Venturi duct with Air entering at the top. The duct narrows to a throat, where streamlines with downward arrows crowd together, and widens again below. The throat is labelled Low pressure. On the left, a chamber labelled Gas, at Atmospheric pressure, is joined to the throat by a bent pipe.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.20: Carburetor of an engine (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.20).

blocks.text: A stream of air passing over a tube dipped in a liquid causes the liquid to rise in the tube. This effect is used in perfume bottles and paint sprayers: when the rubber ball of an atomizer is squeezed the air is blown through the tube and rushes out through the narrow aperture at high speed, causing a fall of pressure, so the atmospheric pressure pushes the perfume up leading to the narrow aperture.

blocks.alt: Air, shown by a blue arrow, enters a line that narrows to a nozzle on the right. A vertical tube dips from the nozzle into a container of red paint; red arrows show the paint rising up the tube and being sprayed out of the nozzle. Blue arrows press down on the paint surface inside the container. Labels: Air, Nozzle, Paint.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.21: A stream of air passing over a tube dipped in a liquid (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.21).

blocks.text: Consider a pipe in which a fluid of density rho flows through different areas of cross-section (Fig. 5.22): A1 at the wide end and A2 at the narrow portion, with flow speeds v1 and v2 and pressures P1 and P2 indicated by the limbs of a manometer. As the pipe is horizontal, the average potential energy is the same at both places, so Bernoulli's equation gives P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2, or P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho v2^2 - (1/2) rho v1^2, or P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho (v2^2 - v1^2) ... (5.25). From the equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2, v1 = A2 v2 / A1. As A2 is small compared with A1, v1 is small compared with v2: the fluid in the wider portion is very slow compared with the narrow portion, so v1 can be neglected on the right-hand side of Eq. 5.25: P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho v2^2 ... (5.26). This is the Venturi relation, used in the Venturi meter, a device to measure the speed of liquid flow. It is clear from Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe that where the speed is high the pressure will be low: P + (1/2) rho v^2 = constant (Interesting Information).

blocks.alt: A horizontal pipe with a wide part A1 on the left, a narrow throat A2 in the middle and a wide part again on the right. Three streamlines squeeze together through the throat; v1 is marked in the wide part and v2 in the throat. A U-tube manometer below joins the wide part and the throat: the level under the wide part, P1, is lower, and the level under the throat, P2, is higher by h.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.22: Venturi meter (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.22).

blocks.text: A simple application of Bernoulli's equation: suppose a large tank of fluid has two small orifices A and B (Fig. 5.23). To find the speed with which water flows from orifice A: since the orifices are so small, the efflux speeds v2 and v3 are much larger than the speed v1 of the top surface of the water, so v1 can be taken as approximately zero. Bernoulli's equation then reads P1 + rho g h1 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2 + rho g h2; but P1 = P2 = atmospheric pressure, so v2 = sqrt(2 g (h1 - h2)) ... (5.27). This is Torricelli's theorem: the speed of efflux is equal to the velocity gained by the fluid in falling through the distance (h1 - h2) under the action of gravity. The speed of efflux is the same as that of a ball falling through the height (h1 - h2): the top level of the tank has moved down a little and the PE has been transferred into the KE of the efflux. If the orifice had been pointed upward at B, this KE would allow the liquid to rise to the level of the water in the tank; in practice viscous-energy losses alter the result to some extent.

blocks.alt: A tall tank of water whose surface, moving down with speed v1, is at height h1 above the bottom. Orifice A on the right, at height h2 above the bottom and h1 - h2 below the surface, lets out a jet with speed v2 that curves down. Orifice B, low on the left, leads into a tube that turns the jet upward (speed v3), and the water rises to the level of the water in the tank.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.23: A tank containing fluid with a orifice (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.23).
